Futuna island has historically been divided between two kingdoms — Sigave on the western coast and Alo (also called Tuʻa) on the east — together with the small uninhabited island of Alofi which falls under Alo. Each is led by a Sau (king) chosen from a defined set of noble lineages, in a more openly elective system than Uvea's Hau. Marist missionary Pierre Chanel was killed at Pōʻī in 1841 by order of king Niuliki of Alo; he was later canonised, and his death is cited by colonial-era French sources as moral pretext for protectorate. The polygon covers Futuna and Alofi only and necessarily includes some ocean. Calling these polities 'tribal' as some 19th-century French sources did effaces real institutional continuity over centuries.

ETHICS-007: The Lapita culture is an archaeological construct identified primarily through a distinctive dentate-stamped pottery tradition. It is NOT a single polity or ethnic group, but rather a shared cultural complex spread across thousands of kilometers of ocean. Representing it as a single entity risks obscuring the diversity of Lapita-associated communities. However, the Lapita expansion represents one of the most remarkable episodes of human exploration and colonization — the settlement of Remote Oceania from the Bismarck Archipelago to Samoa/Tonga in roughly 500 years. The Lapita people are the ancestors of all Polynesian peoples and contributed significantly to the ancestry of Melanesian coastal populations. ETHICS-003: The 'language code' is listed as 'und' (undetermined) because Lapita is a prehistoric culture known only from archaeology; its language(s) are reconstructed as Proto-Oceanic/Proto-Polynesian through historical linguistics, not direct evidence.
